name: Independent vs Coupled Risks
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: It Gets More Complicated: When Risks Are Not Actually Independent
lesson.summary: The joint probability calculation in the previous chapter assumed the seven breakthroughs were independent of one another, but in reality they share underlying physics and engineering constraints, which means their risks are coupled, not independent, and that coupling changes the math in ways that are hard to pin down precisely.
lesson.body:
The multiplication rule from the previous chapter, multiplying individual probabilities together to get a joint probability, only works cleanly when the events involved are truly independent, meaning the outcome of one tells you nothing about the likely outcome of another. That assumption is a useful simplification for illustrating the pattern of compounding requirements, but it is worth being honest that it is probably not accurate for quantum computing's seven breakthroughs, because they do not arise from seven unrelated sources of difficulty. They largely trace back to a smaller number of shared underlying physics and engineering constraints.

Consider coherence time and error rate, two of the breakthroughs from earlier in this course. Both are governed substantially by the same underlying physics: material defects in the superconducting circuits, stray electromagnetic noise, and imperfections in the control electronics. A materials science advance that meaningfully extends how long a qubit stays coherent very often also reduces gate error rates, because the two problems share root causes rather than being separate dice rolls. That means "coherence improves" and "error rates drop" are correlated, not independent: progress on one is evidence, not proof, of progress on the other, and the same goes in reverse for setbacks. The same logic connects connectivity and cryogenics from this chapter's earlier material: the same dense, low-heat control electronics needed to make cryogenics scale to more qubits are also what would make new connectivity topologies, like tunable couplers placed close to the chip, practical to build.

Coupling like this can cut in two different directions, and it is important not to assume it automatically makes things worse. If several breakthroughs share a single underlying bottleneck, say a materials science limit that nobody has found a way around, then that one stalled bottleneck could hold back multiple breakthroughs at once, making the whole bundle more fragile than independent multiplication would suggest. But coupling can also work the other way: a single deep breakthrough, say a new class of superconducting material with far lower defect density, could simultaneously improve coherence, lower error rates, and ease the cryogenics wiring problem all at once, making the bundle easier to achieve together than treating each piece as an isolated coin flip would suggest.

The honest takeaway is not a cleaner number, it is humility about the number from the previous chapter. The multiplication in the joint probability chapter is genuinely useful for showing why requiring several breakthroughs at once is harder than requiring just one, but it is a demonstration of a reasoning pattern, not a precise forecast, and coupling is exactly the reason why. Reasonable, informed people can disagree about whether the shared physics behind these seven breakthroughs makes the overall bundle more or less likely to succeed together than naive independent multiplication implies. What nobody can honestly do is skip past that uncertainty and hand you a single confident percentage, for either the individual breakthroughs or the bundle as a whole.
